entries.title: Illinois cannabis consumption rises as state tax revenues dip
entries.summary: <p>Illinois’ cannabis industry saw a big drop in sales numbers over the last year, but it’s not because demand or product sales dropped, a new state report shows.</p><p>According to the report released by the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation’s Cannabis Regulation and Oversight Office, total dispensary sales dropped to about $1.5 billion in fiscal year 2026.</p><p>That’s down from nearly $2 billion in sales in 2025.</p><p>But that downward financial shift came despite an uptick in demand. Monthly sales figures show more than 5 million adult-use cannabis items sold in July 2026, marking a record high. August sales totaled nearly 4.9 million adult-use items, a 9% increase in items sold compared to last year.</p><p>According to the oversight office, there are more dispensaries, and the product is more accessible, so the number of items sold is still going up.</p><p>But the industry still saw its gross revenues slide, the report said, because of a growing supply of legal cannabis in the market that has caused prices to drop and because of frequent promotional sales by dispensaries.</p><p>The hit to the state treasury has been less severe.</p><p>Cannabis taxes generated more than $456 million in tax revenue for the state, slightly down from last year’s $474 million, according to the Illinois Department of Revenue.</p><p>The report also shows a slight increase in licensed dispensaries, with 29 new licenses issued this year.</p><p>The new financial numbers from the state come after the Illinois Hemp Act took effect in June. The law, which passed out of the General Assembly during this year’s spring legislative session, imposed new safeguards to keep hemp and cannabis products out of the hands of minors.</p><p>It also allows more dispensaries to opt-in on selling medical-use cannabis, permitting telehealth-verified patients access to cannabis and allowing dispensaries to use curbside and drive-through sales methods.</p><p>Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer Erin Johnson said the newly released report helps identify issues in regulation.</p><p>“The data collected this year is a snapshot of cannabis regulation just as we begin to see the impact from last legislative session’s important reforms,” she said.</p><p>In addition to opening pathways for dispensaries to supply medical cannabis, the Illinois Hemp Act created new mandatory licensing and standards for CBD manufacturers,and a pathway for hemp businesses entering the licensed cannabis market.</p><p>And dispensary operators can have license renewal fees waived or reduced based on how much they make.</p><p>Johnson said the law is already positively affecting the Illinois cannabis market by allowing all dispensaries to serve medical patients, modernizing possession limits, and reducing the regulatory burden on cannabis businesses.</p>
entries.author: Isabela Nieto

entries.title: Defendant in fatal stabbing of CTA janitor was on electronic monitoring, prosecutors say
entries.summary: <p>The man charged with murder in the fatal stabbing of a Chicago Transit Authority janitor last week was already on electronic monitoring as part of his probation for two felony cases, prosecutors said in court Sunday.</p><p>Chevazz Campbell, 37, was ordered detained at a hearing Sunday, where prosecutors told a Cook County judge he argued with and slung racial slurs at CTA employees before macing and fatally stabbing Julian Mobley, a CTA janitor.</p><p>Campbell entered the Damen Green Line station around 3 p.m. Thursday and tried to jump the gate without paying, prosecutors said. He argued with a CTA employee sitting inside a kiosk, using racial slurs, prosecutors alleged.</p><p>Mobley was working nearby and also argued with Campbell as he took the escalator to the train platform, prosecutors said. Campbell then came back downstairs and left the station, and took something out of his bag before going back inside, surveillance video shows, according to prosecutors.</p><p>Campbell approached Mobley and sprayed him in the face with mace twice, prosecutors said. Mobley ran away and Campbell chased after him, then stabbed him once in the neck with a knife he took from his bag, prosecutors said.</p><p>Mobley ran into a janitor's closet, gushing blood from his neck, prosecutors said.</p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital and pronounced dead.</p><p>Cook County State's Attorney Eileen O'Neill Burke and president of ATU Local 308, the union that represents CTA workers, including Mobley, released a joint statement calling for changes to the state's electronic monitoring system. Campbell had violated his curfew at least four times before the stabbing, they said in the statement.</p><p>"The failures of our electronic monitoring system could not be clearer: there is not effective monitoring or proactive enforcement when someone is unaccounted for, and that poses a grave risk to public safety," they said in the statement. "We need a permanent legislative solution to close these gaps, strengthen accountability, and better protect people like Julian, who deserve to be safe on the job and return home to their families after work.”</p><p>Campbell fled the scene with Mobley's CTA identification card and cellphone, which he picked up after Mobley dropped them during the incident. They were both found in a storm drain that Campbell was seen bending down next to after he left the scene, prosecutors said.</p><p>Campbell then stopped at a convenience store, where he turned his jacket inside out, gave the store clerk his duffel bag and asked to borrow a hat, presumably trying to disguise himself.</p><p>He surrendered later that night and was identified on surveillance video by someone who has known him most of his life, prosecutors said.<br></p>

You can follow along on X <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien" target="_blank" >@michaelsobrien</a> or read the previews here. All Illinois schools are eligible, not just schools in the Sun-Times’ coverage area. Please include the following:</p><p>School:<br>Coach:<br>Phone number:<br>Outlook for this season:<br>Top Returning Players (Position, Height, Year in school):<br>Top Newcomers (Position, Height, Year in school):<br>Top teams in your conference:<br>Players on your team and in the conference to consider for the list of the area’s best:<br>Interesting story idea about your team:</p><p><i>This story will be updated nearly every day until the start of the season. Here’s everything that has been sent out so far:</i></p><p><b>Deerfield:</b> Jack DiMatteo takes over as coach after the best season in school history. Eleven seniors return, including leading scorer Gray Kanter and fellow starters Zach Baum, Peter Dimitriou and Max Stevens.</p><p><b>Naperville North:</b> Young group improved over the summer. Defense and rebounding will be key. Senior guard Jack Zitko is the lone returning starter. Sixth man Reid Montanari, a 6-5 senior, will step up. Nolan Scarbrough will have an expanded role and Clark Roush, Sam Steele and soph Toby Kapusta are the top newcomers. </p><p><b>Schaumburg:</b> New coach Garrett Gatz has just one starter back, 6-3 junior Masyn Harrell. Seniors Aaron Shogren, Donovan Manning and Caden Williams will play important roles.</p>

entries.title: Ben Johnson's loss was disconcerting for reasons that go beyond the Packers rivalry
entries.summary: <p>The most disconcerting loss of Ben Johnson’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> career had everything Sunday — an offense that never found its rhythm, a defense that got beat by the deep ball and every turn and a special teams unit that missed its only field goal. There was a way-too-late quarterback switch and a pass rush that popped up for one out of 60 minutes.</p><p></p><p>The Bears never led, spending more than half the time trailing by two touchdowns in a game they’d lose 31-7. They committed five turnovers for the first time in three years to lose their sixth regular-season NFC North game in eight tries dating to last year. Bears players had their words thrown in their faces by the Packers, whose season was revived — saved? — on a day when their rival could have put them in their rear-view mirror. Even the postgame showers were cold, but just in the visitor’s locker room.</p><p></p><p>Johnson spent Monday trying to sort through what happened.</p><p></p><p>“We’ve got to be critical of ourselves, look in the mirror a little bit [Monday] and get that cleaned up and fixed,” Johnson said. “We’ve had some good meetings already. Looking forward to cleaning up our mess and fixing everything we need to fix as we prepare for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/12/bears-falcons-coach-kevin-stefanski-michael-penix-availability-tua-tagovailoa-nfl" target="_blank" >Atlanta</a>.”</p><p></p><p>What a mess it was.</p><p></p><p><b>“</b>It’s run game, pass game — wasn’t what it was supposed to look like,” Johnson said. “And then cleaning up those explosive plays on defense.”</p><p></p><p>Fixing it will be the fiercest challenge of Johnson’s season, if not his young coaching career. Johnson’s most personal head-coaching loss was the 31-point shellacking he took in his Ford Field homecoming last year. But that was in his second-ever game as head coach, when no one expected his scheme or style to be fully formed.</p><p></p><p>Sunday’s blowout at the hands of his rival, by contrast, came with the Bears favored to win at Lambeau Field for the first time in 20 years. Expectations were different. The disappointment was greater.</p><p></p><p>Being humiliated by the rival Packers is a red flag that his predecessors haven’t had to confront in years. Matt Eberflus never lost by as many as 24 points at Lambeau Field. Neither did Matt Nagy or John Fox. The last time the Bears were so outclassed in Green Bay was a 55-14 loss in 2014 that set Marc Trestman down the road to unemployment. No one is suggesting Johnson is on that path. He won the NFC North last year and deserves credit for leading the Bears to consecutive victories with two different backups under center. It was clear after beating the Eagles and Jets that the star of the offense was the offense itself — and the man calling the plays. By that rationale, the reason the offense sputtered so greatly Sunday was the same man.</p><p></p><p>The Bears’ quarterback play will improve soon enough, whether Caleb Williams returns for Sunday’s game against the Falcons or the following Thursday against the Patriots. The same can’t be said for a two-faced defense that has given up 68 points over two games this season — and just 28 over the other three.</p><p></p><p>Johnson took responsibility for the Bears’ offensive play-calling and said coordinator Dennis Allen did the same on defense Monday after allowing Packers quarterback Jordan Love to throw for 367 yards.</p><p></p><p>“He’ll be the first one to tell you when there’s a bad call,” Johnson said. “But also [there were] a combination of bad rushes mixed in there. And bad coverage mixed in there. So really all three things showed up over the course of the game.”</p><p></p><p>To paraphrase something Fox said years ago: it was all a problem.</p><p></p><p>The worst part is who it was against — and how that affects the Bears’ postseason chances. The Bears went 2-4 in the North last season and still somehow found a way to win it. That won’t happen again.</p><p></p><p>The Bears are 3-2, yet last in the NFC North, the result of losing both their divisional games this season. The Vikings, who many thought were the worst team in the North, are 5-0 this season. The Packers are Lions are each 3-2. The former knew what was at stake, beyond just rivalry bragging rights, on Sunday.</p><p></p><p>“Against an NFC North opponent, against the Bears,” Love said. “We needed this one.”</p><p></p><p>The easiest path to the playoffs is to beat up on your division. Since Johnson took over, though, the Vikings lead the NFC North with a 6-2 record. The Packers are 5-3 and the Lions 2-4. The Bears are 2-6.</p><p></p><p>Johnson has won 25% of his regular-season divisional games, the same as Trestman. He could win his next five NFC North contests and still have a worse divisional winning percentage than Nagy did the day he was fired.</p><p></p><p>Johnson has been outscored by 66 points in eight games against the Packers, Lions and Vikings in his head coaching career. Outside the division, he’s a whopping 12-2, outscoring opponents by 115 points.</p><p></p><p>Sunday stung, then, for reasons that go beyond the 214-game rivalry series.</p><p></p><p>Johnson won’t have a chance to improve his divisional record until Thanksgiving, when he returns to Ford Field. By then, he might have new problems to fix.</p><p></p><p><b>“</b>We’re a 3-2 football team,” Johnson said. “The part that stinks is that we’re 0-2 in the division right now. So we dug ourselves in a hole.”<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: If Bears QB Caleb Williams is out vs. Falcons, Case Keenum should start over Tyson Bagent
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ confidence in backup quarterback Tyson Bagent prompted questions about whether he one day could be a starter. But coach Ben Johnson faced a drastically different question Monday after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/11/bears-coach-ben-johnson-runs-out-of-answers-unable-to-ignite-offense-in-31-7-loss-to-packers" target="_blank" >benching him in the Bears’ 31-7 meltdown against the Packers</a>:</p><p>Is Bagent a capable backup?</p><p>Johnson replied defiantly that all three of his quarterbacks — injured starter Caleb Williams, Bagent and veteran third-stringer Case Keenum — are winners, but the fact that it had to be asked showed how sharply the outlook on Bagent has flipped after two starts.</p><p>Johnson also didn’t answer whether, if Williams remains out, Bagent or Keenum would be his first-team quarterback at practice Wednesday. His evasion said plenty. If he is sure of all three, it would have been easy for him to name one.</p><p>If Williams isn’t healthy enough to play Sunday at the Falcons, Johnson needs to go back to Keenum.</p><p>The Bears must set aside whatever loyalty they have to Bagent and their intrigue about whether he can develop into a valuable trade asset. This is a vital game for them, considering the teams who played in the Super Bowl last season are looming after the Falcons.</p><p>Johnson will weigh the total body of work, but Keenum has made a stronger argument in games than Bagent. Bagent completed 12 of 21 passes for 87 yards with two interceptions for a 27.4 passer rating — the worst by a Bears starter since Caleb Hanie in 2011 — against the Packers before Johnson sent in Keenum at the start of the fourth quarter.</p><p>The interceptions were brutal, and that was an issue the week before, too, when the Bears beat the Jets. Bagent posted an 83.9 passer rating on 25-for-34 passing for 268 yards with an interception, but three other picks were negated by penalties.</p><p>The top responsibility for a backup quarterback is to do no harm, to avoid dicey throws and to secure the ball in the pocket. Keenum failed to check those boxes Sunday, as well, with an interception on a desperate throw at the goal line and a lost fumble when the game already was decided.</p><p>Bagent’s interceptions were more his fault than they were great plays by defenders. When he threw into double coverage for wide receiver Luther Burden to the right in the first quarter, safety Javon Bullard broke up the pass and safety Xavier McKinney caught the deflection.</p><p>Johnson said Monday that Bagent should have recognized Burden was blanketed and gone elsewhere. He bypassed a checkdown to running back Roschon Johnson on his left and missed wide receiver Kalif Raymond potentially sprinting into open space deeper down the left side.</p><p>The interception that broke Johnson’s patience came late in the third quarter, when the Packers fooled Bagent into thinking they were in Cover 0 before the snap but actually were playing Cover 2. McKinney was waiting when he tried to hit tight end Colston Loveland over the middle.</p><p>‘‘He didn’t make those same type of throws over the course of camp,’’ Johnson said.</p><p>It turns out there’s a big difference between practice and games.</p><p>Bagent has more arm strength and athleticism than Keenum does at 38, but he made mistakes the last two weeks in coverage recognition and decision-making. Keenum’s experience makes him sharper in those departments.</p><p>Neither option is particularly alluring, but the Bears must resist the temptation to rush Williams back. That’s a bad idea. It would be better to endure this for one more game than to rush him onto the field and risk a setback that would keep him out longer.</p><p>If the Bears take it cautiously, as they should with a player they think is their franchise quarterback, they’ll be hesitant to play Williams twice in five days — the Bears host the Patriots the next Thursday — coming off a Grade 2 strained hamstring. The soundest plan is to hope for the best with Keenum in Atlanta and target the game against the Patriots for Williams’ return.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Connor Bedard's return alters a Blackhawks power play that needed altering
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> captain Connor Bedard is trending toward making his season debut Tuesday against the Penguins after taking part in another full practice Monday, coach Jeff Blashill said.</p><p>Bedard’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/11/connor-bedard-blackhawks-return-imminent-patrick-kane" target="_blank" >return</a> after just six games missed — about half as many as his initial recovery timeline suggested — should inject talent, fire and life into almost every aspect of the struggling Hawks.</p><p>The power play sits at the top of that list. It desperately needs a spark after two toothless weeks, and Bedard’s return would represent a big one.</p><p>Bedard will slot in on the left side of the top power-play unit, allowing Patrick Kane to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/21/blackhawks-power-play-patrick-kane-roman-kantserov-bowen-byram" target="_blank" >shift back</a> to the right, where he has spent the vast majority of his career. That positions both players to fire one-timers off passes from Bowen Byram (at the point), Roman Kantserov (in the bumper) and Tyler Bertuzzi (down low).</p><p>The Hawks previously had only Anton Frondell in a one-timer position, and Bedard’s return will bump him down to the second unit.</p><p>‘‘For sure, Bedard on the power play [is] a mega-weapon,’’ Blashill said. ‘‘You lose Frondell, who I think is going to be a mega-weapon. There’s still a learning process. I think Anton has played great hockey, but on the power play, he hasn’t played great. He’s played OK, and he’s not alone in that.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Jeff Blashill on Connor Bedard:<br><br>“He came back last year and still had restrictions on him: no faceoffs and things like that. There’s mental hurdles involved with that. With this one being surgically repaired, it’s in a great spot.”<br><br>But he cautioned it’s “not easy to just jump…</p>— Ben Pope (@BenPopeCST) <a href="https://x.com/BenPopeCST/status/2109703039053631846?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 12, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Hawks’ power play is 1-for-14 right now. Their lone goal came from Sam Rinzel on the second unit. They’ve attempted only 23 shots on those 14 opportunities, and only 10 have made it on goal. They also have allowed six short-handed shots on goal and one short-handed goal. Those are awful numbers.</p><p>Blashill pointed out the power play has set up great looks for Byram in each of the last two games, only for Byram’s stick to snap in both instances. Luck, of course, plays a role in any hot or cold streak. Nevertheless, things need to change.</p><p>Kane insisted Monday he ‘‘didn’t feel too bad on the left’’ side of the power play, but he admitted the unit in general has felt ‘‘a little bit off.’’ He’s certainly not upset about moving back to the right.</p><p>He also mentioned how penalty kills have improved at eliminating seam passes from one flank to the other since the earlier years of his career. Moving the puck from side to side now usually requires using the point man, and Bedard’s and Kane’s handedness should help Byram with that.</p><p>‘‘It’s a little easier for me, having two forehands on each side,’’ Byram said. ‘‘Teams pressure hard, so even those extra couple of inches . . . makes a big difference.’’</p><p>Power-play success in 2026 often involves getting initial shots through on goal, then retrieving rebounds and loose pucks to generate second and third chances. Kane said he doesn’t think the Hawks have done that well enough.</p><p>‘‘We [would] get the first chance, and then it would be down the ice,’’ he said. ‘‘And then you break out and get another chance, and it would be down the ice. We weren’t able to really have sustained pressure.’’</p><p>Blashill disagreed with that somewhat, blaming the power-play struggles on ‘‘unforced errors’’ and inaccurate passes more than on a lack of retrievals, given that Kantserov and Bertuzzi are decent retrievers.</p><p>He also mentioned winning faceoffs and breaking into the zone cleanly as other keys.</p><p>Anecdotally, the Hawks’ break-ins haven’t looked smooth. And data shows they’re struggling on power-play faceoffs, ranking 29th in the NHL at 40.7%. That’s even worse than their overall faceoff percentage of 42.4%, which ranks last.</p><p>Blashill critiqued the NHL’s unreliable faceoff tracking, but those numbers match what one would expect from the Hawks’ inexperienced cast of centers. That’s another area in which Bedard’s return could be of major help — provided his faceoff success continues on the upward trajectory he set last season, that is.</p>
